title: India Fires Back at Navarro's Russian Oil Attacks as US-India Trade Tensions Persist
excerpt: New Delhi has rejected White House trade adviser Peter Navarro's accusations of profiteering from Russian crude as 'inaccurate and misleading,' even as record oil imports cloud a fragile trade deal.
body:
• White House trade adviser Peter Navarro has escalated rhetoric against India over Russian oil, calling it a "laundromat for the Kremlin" and the Ukraine conflict "Modi's war"
  • India's Oil Minister Hardeep Puri and Ministry of External Affairs have firmly rejected the allegations as "inaccurate and misleading"
  • Despite a February 2026 trade deal that cut US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18%, India's Russian oil imports hit a record 2.8 million barrels per day in July
  • Planned US-India trade talks in New Delhi were called off, clouding prospects for resolution

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro has unleashed a sustained campaign against India's purchases of Russian crude oil, drawing a sharp and coordinated response from New Delhi that has added a volatile new dimension to already strained US-India trade relations.

In an opinion piece published in the Financial Times, Navarro called India's Russian oil purchases "opportunistic and deeply corrosive" and accused New Delhi of acting as "a global clearinghouse for Russian oil, converting embargoed crude into high-value exports while giving Moscow the dollars it needs." He went further in broadcast interviews, labeling the Ukraine conflict "Modi's war" and describing India as "nothing but a laundromat for the Kremlin."

India Pushes Back Hard

India's response was swift and unsparing. Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, writing in The Hindu newspaper, rejected Navarro's charges point by point. "Some critics allege that India has become a 'laundromat' for Russian oil. Nothing could be further from the truth," Puri wrote, noting that India has long been the world's fourth-largest exporter of petroleum products and that its export volumes and refining margins have remained "broadly the same" since before the Ukraine war.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2087357149890695578

"Every transaction has used legal shipping and insurance, compliant traders and audited channels. India has not broken rules. India has stabilised markets and kept global prices from spiralling."

— Hardeep Singh Puri, India's Oil Minister

The Ministry of External Affairs went further, formally calling Navarro's statements "inaccurate and misleading." MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal pointed out that Russian oil purchases are not sanctioned and fall under the G-7/EU price cap system designed to keep oil flowing while capping Moscow's revenues.

Navarro's remark about "Brahmins profiteering at the expense of the Indian people" drew particular outrage, with Indian analysts condemning it as casteist and culturally offensive. Even on X, community notes fact-checked his posts, noting that India's oil trade was "for energy security, not just profit" and did not violate any sanctions. Navarro dismissed the fact-checks as "crap" and accused Elon Musk of "letting propaganda into people's posts."

The Tariff Roller Coaster

The rhetorical clash has played out against dramatic tariff shifts. Last August, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Indian goods — 25% reciprocal and 25% specifically targeting India's Russian oil purchases. Navarro repeatedly backed the punitive rate, telling Bloomberg Television that India was "cozying up to Xi Jinping."

A breakthrough appeared to come in February 2026, when President Trump announced a trade deal cutting tariffs to 18% after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi reportedly agreed to halt Russian crude imports. Trump signed an executive order removing the Russia-related tariff, citing India's commitment to stop direct and indirect Russian oil purchases.

The deal's promise has not held. India's Russian oil imports surged to a record 2.8 million barrels per day in July 2026 — over a third of its total crude imports — according to trade data. A planned visit by US trade negotiators to New Delhi, scheduled for August 25-29, was abruptly called off, dashing hopes of further progress.

Caught in the Crossfire

For Indian Americans, the dispute carries personal weight. The US-India relationship underpins everything from H-1B visa programs to defense cooperation and technology transfers. Navarro's warning that it was "risky to transfer cutting-edge US military capabilities" to India while it strengthened ties with Russia and China signals a potential chilling effect on the broader strategic partnership that 4.4 million Indian Americans depend on.

Trump himself has oscillated between warmth and pressure. At a White House press conference, he called Modi "a great Prime Minister" and said the two countries have "a special relationship," while maintaining the tariff threat. Modi reciprocated on X, writing that he "deeply appreciates and fully reciprocates President Trump's sentiments."

What Comes Next

India has made clear it views energy purchases as a sovereign matter, with the MEA stating that New Delhi "will take all necessary measures to safeguard its national interests and economic security." Analysts note that China, the largest buyer of Russian crude at 47% of exports, has faced far less criticism from Navarro — selective targeting that India's defenders call illogical.

With trade negotiations stalled, India's oil imports from Russia at record levels, and Navarro showing no sign of softening his tone, the dispute appears headed for further escalation. The next flashpoint may come if the Trump administration moves to reimpose the Russia-related tariffs that were lifted in the February deal.
nri_angle: The US-India oil dispute threatens the broader strategic partnership that underpins H-1B programs, defense cooperation, and technology transfers for Indian Americans.
